title: Cold open: 8:13 pm
text:
[low, close] Eight-thirteen in the evening. About ten thousand feet above the forests of southwest Washington.
In the cockpit, the crew feel a small jolt. The tail lifts.
[beat] At the back of the plane, the stairs are open to the rain. And the man who opened them is gone.
[pause] He has two hundred thousand dollars strapped to his body. He's wearing a business suit and loafers.
[softly] And for more than fifty years, nobody has been able to say who he was.

title: Portland
text:
[warm, unhurried] Portland, Oregon. The day before Thanksgiving, nineteen seventy-one.
A man in a dark suit buys a one-way ticket to Seattle. A thirty-minute flight. He pays cash.
He gives his name as Dan Cooper.
[beat] Keep that name in mind. It's our first clue. And it's wrong in more ways than one.

title: The note
text:
[natural storytelling] He orders a bourbon and soda. Lights a cigarette. Just after takeoff, he hands a flight attendant a folded note.
She thinks it's his phone number, and pockets it without reading it.
[pause] He leans over.

title: The demands
text:
[tense] In his briefcase: red cylinders, wires, a battery.
He wants two hundred thousand dollars. Four parachutes. And a fuel truck waiting in Seattle.
The plane circles for two hours while the FBI gathers the cash. Ten thousand twenty-dollar bills.
[beat] And before they hand it over, agents photograph every single one. Every serial number.
Remember that, too.

title: The exchange
text:
[natural storytelling] In Seattle, he trades the passengers for the money and the parachutes.
Then he gives the crew a very specific flight plan. Head for Mexico. Fly low, below ten thousand feet. Landing gear down. Flaps lowered. As slow as the plane can go.
And the rear stairs… open.
[pause] It's an odd set of instructions. Not something most people would think to ask for.
[beat] Which brings us to clue number two.

title: The jump
text:
[natural storytelling] Seven-forty. They take off again. He sends the last flight attendant to the cockpit. She looks back, and sees him tying something around his waist.
Eight o'clock. A red light. The stairs are down.
[pause] Eight-thirteen. [very quiet] The jolt.
[long pause]
Two hours later, they land in Reno. The cabin is empty. He's taken the money and the briefcase. He's left behind two parachutes, a few cigarette butts, and a black clip-on tie.

title: The case board
text:
[natural storytelling] That night, one of the longest investigations in FBI history begins. And it starts with almost nothing.
No face. No real name. No body. No parachute.
[beat] Just a handful of clues. Let's go through them, one at a time.

title: Clue 1: the name
text:
[natural storytelling] Police question a man in Portland whose name really is D.B. Cooper. He has nothing to do with it. But a reporter hears the name, and the hijacker who called himself Dan becomes "D.B." Cooper. A name that was never his.
[pause] Years later, investigators notice something else. In the nineteen-fifties and sixties there was a popular comic book about a heroic Canadian air force pilot. His name was Dan Cooper.
[beat] The comic was published in French. Never in English.
So did our man pick a random name? Or had he spent time in Europe or Canada… and borrowed his alias from a hero who parachutes out of planes?

title: Clue 2: what he knew
text:
[natural storytelling] Look at what he asked for. Four parachutes, not one. Possibly so the FBI wouldn't dare give him a faulty one, in case he took someone with him.
A speed and flap setting that suited a jump. And the rear stairs.
[pause] The Boeing seven-twenty-seven was one of the few airliners you could jump from in flight. Very few people knew that. Some researchers point out that the same type of plane had been used for secret parachute drops in Southeast Asia.
On the way, he even recognised Tacoma from the air, and knew where the air force base was.
[beat] This was not a random man with a random plan. He knew planes. Maybe the military.

title: Clue 3: the night
text:
[natural storytelling] Now picture the jump. At night. In rain. Into a freezing wind. Over dense forest, with no lights below.
In a business suit. And loafers.
[pause] The FBI agent who led the case, Ralph Himmelsbach, was a pilot himself. He never believed Cooper survived. Neither did the agents who came after him.
And one of the two parachutes he jumped with was a training reserve. Sewn shut. Useless. An expert might have noticed.
[beat] But here's the thing. Hundreds of soldiers searched those woods, twice. Not one of them found a body. Or a parachute.

title: Clue 4: the money
text:
[natural storytelling] Remember the serial numbers. The FBI sent the list to banks, casinos and businesses across the country.
If Cooper spent his money, a bill should turn up somewhere. A store. A bank. A racetrack.
[pause] As far as we know, not one ever did.
[beat] For eight years, not a single bill from the ransom was found anywhere.
And then, in nineteen eighty, some of it was.

title: Clue 5: the river
text:
[natural storytelling] February, nineteen eighty. An eight-year-old boy is digging on a sandy bank of the Columbia River. He finds bundles of old twenty-dollar bills, rotting, still held together.
Five thousand eight hundred dollars. And the serial numbers match.
[pause] It should have solved the case. It made it stranger.
The geologist who studied the site believed the money arrived years after the hijacking, above a layer of dredged sand. Others have since challenged that.
And in twenty twenty, a scientist found microscopic algae on the bills. A kind that blooms in spring. Not in November, when Cooper jumped.
[beat] So how did a bundle of Cooper's money end up in the river, months or years later… and only part of it?

title: Clue 6: the tie
text:
[natural storytelling] The last clue is the one he left behind. The black tie.
In two thousand one, the FBI pulled a partial DNA profile from it. Then in the twenty-tens, a team of volunteer scientists looked at the tie under an electron microscope.
They found more than a hundred thousand tiny particles. Including pure titanium, and the rare earth metal cerium. In nineteen seventy-one, those were used in only a few places. Like aerospace plants.
[beat] Places where engineers wore ties to work.
[pause] The FBI's answer was careful. They don't know for sure the tie was his.

title: The suspects
text: [natural storytelling] Over the years, the FBI looked at more than eight hundred suspects. Five of them come up again and again. All of them have died. None was ever proven to be Cooper.

title: Suspect 1: the copycat
text:
[natural storytelling] Five months after Cooper, a man hijacked another seven-twenty-seven, took half a million dollars, and jumped out over Utah. Same method. Same stairs.
Richard McCoy. A former soldier, a skydiver. He was caught within days.
[pause] Perfect fit? The FBI said no. McCoy was twenty-nine, and he didn't match what the two flight attendants described. Some researchers still argue about it.

title: Suspect 2: the insider
text:
[natural storytelling] Kenneth Christiansen worked for the very airline that was hijacked. He had been a paratrooper. About a year after the hijacking, he bought a house, reportedly with cash. After he died, his own brother came to suspect him.
[pause] But he was shorter and slighter than the man on the plane, and the FBI did not find enough to name him.

title: Suspect 3: the deathbed
text:
[natural storytelling] Duane Weber, on his deathbed, reportedly told his wife: "I'm Dan Cooper." She didn't know what it meant.
[beat] The FBI compared his DNA with the profile from the tie. It didn't match.

title: Suspect 4: the soldier
text:
[natural storytelling] Robert Rackstraw. A Vietnam veteran with parachute training. Decades later, a team of amateur investigators built a case around him, and he became one of the best-known suspects of all.
[pause] But in nineteen seventy-one he was only twenty-eight. The FBI had questioned him in the seventies, and dropped him as a suspect. He always denied it.

title: Suspect 5: the one who never existed
text:
[natural storytelling] And then there's the suspect most investigators favour. A man whose name we've never heard. Who died that night in the forest. And who was never missed by anyone who connected him to a hijacking.
[beat] He fits every clue. Which is exactly the problem.

title: Three endings
text:
[natural storytelling] So here are the endings. Pick one.
[pause] One. He didn't make it. He landed in the dark, in the cold, somewhere in that forest. And the forest kept him.
[pause] Two. He made it. He walked out of the woods, hid the money, and lived a quiet life, knowing something nobody else knew.
[pause] Three. Something in between. He made it to the river, or the money did. And the river kept the rest.
[beat] Every one of them fits some of the clues. None of them fits all.

title: Closed
text:
[natural storytelling] In twenty sixteen, after forty-five years, the FBI stopped actively investigating. It's still the only unsolved hijacking in American commercial aviation.
But the case board never really came down. People are still out there. Checking the river. Testing the tie. Reading the old files.

title: The last question
text:
[softly] Somewhere out there is the answer. A name. A grave. Or a bundle of twenty-dollar bills, still waiting in the sand.
[long pause] He planned everything. Except one thing he couldn't control.
[beat] Whether we'd ever stop looking.
